data.title: Under Armour forecasts mid-single-digit revenue decline while maintaining $140M-$160M adjusted operating income outlook
data.description:
Earnings Call Insights: Under Armour (UAA) Q1 fiscal 2027

Management View

  • "We're lowering our revenue outlook for the year while maintaining our adjusted operating income expectation." (CEO Kevin Plank)
  • "Consumer demand remains softer than we expected, particularly in North America and Asia Pacific." (CEO Plank)
  • "We're testing more full-price product in this environment." (CEO Plank)
  • "Building on the 25% reduction we've already achieved in our fall/winter '26 assortment compared to just 2 years ago, we've begun targeting a further 25% SKU reduction over the next 18 months." (CEO Plank)
  • "Launched in May, Bouncy has exceeded expectations while selling at its full $65 retail price." (CEO Plank)
  • "Given this amplified focus, we're taking marketing lower as a percentage of revenue this year." (CEO Plank)
  • "Revenue declined 3% to $1.1 billion." (CFO Reza Taleghani)
  • "Gross margin increased 590 basis points year-over-year to 54.1% in the first quarter." (CFO Taleghani)
  • "Adjusted operating income was $52 million, exceeding our outlook of $30 million to $40 million." (CFO Taleghani)

Outlook

  • "We now expect this year's revenue to decline at a mid-single-digit rate, but we are maintaining our adjusted operating income outlook of $140 million to $160 million." (CFO Taleghani)
  • "We continue to expect expansion of approximately 220 to 270 basis points versus last year" on gross margin, including "roughly 150 basis points of benefit" from IEEPA tariff refunds. (CFO Taleghani)
  • "We've also updated our outlook for adjusted SG&A, which we now expect to decline at a low single-digit rate versus last year." (CFO Taleghani)
  • "For the second quarter, we expect revenue to decline at a high single-digit rate" and "second quarter adjusted operating income of $10 million to $20 million and an adjusted diluted loss per share of $0.01 to $0.03." (CFO Taleghani)

Financial Results

  • "Revenue declined 3% to $1.1 billion" with "North America revenue decreased 9%," "EMEA revenue increased 12%," and "revenue in APAC decreased 7%." (CFO Taleghani)
  • "Direct-to-consumer revenue decreased 6% in the quarter" including "a 12% decline in e-com." (CFO Taleghani)
  • "Footwear revenue was down 8%" and "our run business was flat in the quarter." (CFO Taleghani)
  • "First quarter diluted earnings per share was breakeven" and "our adjusted diluted earnings per share for the quarter was $0.05." (CFO Taleghani)
  • "We ended the quarter with $1.1 billion in inventory, down 3% year-over-year" and "$396 million in cash." (CFO Taleghani)
  • "We completed an amendment to our revolving credit facility earlier this week" and "the amendment is leverage neutral and not related to near-term funding need." (CFO Taleghani)

Q&A

  • Jay Sole, UBS: asked about the Bouncy Tee’s intentionality and repeatability; CEO Plank: "we wanted something that could really demonstrate the full price nature of Under Armour" and "this becomes the metaphor of the plan" for future launches.
  • Jay Sole, UBS: asked how UA can cut sales guidance but keep discipline on margins/inventory; CEO Plank: "we can increase the efficacy" of spend and "we are finding leverage in the business."
  • Sam Poser, Williams Trading: pressed on what “sportswear” means and how big it is; CEO Plank: sportswear is "a product that were intended to be worn with all the performance attributes of UA" in non-sport settings, and Bouncy Tee "walks the line."
  • Sam Poser, Williams Trading: challenged SKU reduction and implications for inventory/promotions; CEO Plank: "there is going to be some near-term trade-off" and CFO Taleghani: "you can do that in the natural sales cycle."
  • Robert Drbul, BTIG: asked what changed over 90 days on revenue and what marketing is focused on; CEO Plank: traffic "precipitously got weaker" from "mid- to late May" and marketing needs to be "more coordinated" to convert sports moments into sales.
  • Brooke Roach, Goldman Sachs: asked if North America pullback is strategic vs. macro and about wholesale cancellations; CFO Taleghani: Q2 reflects macro trends, back half improvement is tied to "product launches" and "continued marketplace discipline."
  • John Elias, on for Guggenheim: asked what offsets lower revenue to hold operating income; CFO Taleghani: "we are basically saying that we're going to do better" on SG&A and "we overdelivered on Q1."
  • Brian Nagel, Oppenheimer: asked whether weakness is across products and about marketing spend; CEO Plank: "we do have great product right now" but must improve storytelling, and CFO Taleghani: marketing will be "at the lower end" of the 10% to 11% range, implying "a reduction in absolute dollars."
  • Peter McGoldrick, Stifel: asked about capital structure and IEEPA refunds; CFO Taleghani: "the IEEPA refunds have come in" and UA expects "free cash flow positive this year" and "There's no M&A on the horizon."

Sentiment Analysis

  • Slightly negative: analysts repeatedly pressed on the revenue guide cut, North America/China demand, promotional intensity, and the mechanics of maintaining profit with lower sales (e.g., Brooke Roach asking how much is macro vs. proactive, and Sam Poser challenging whether inventory should fall faster than sales).
  • Neutral to slightly positive: management emphasized discipline and avoided promising a near-term demand inflection, repeatedly stating "We're not going to chase the market down" (CEO Plank) while defending profit protection through cost control and marketing efficiency.
  • Compared with last quarter, management language shifted from expecting marketing investment to "move higher" to "taking marketing lower as a percentage of revenue" (CEO Plank), while analysts’ questioning in the current call focused more on demand deterioration since late May and promotion pressure.

Quarter-over-Quarter Comparison

  • Current call: "lowering our revenue outlook for the year" (CEO Plank) versus the prior call’s full-year framing that revenue would be "down slightly" (CFO Taleghani, prior transcript).
  • Marketing stance changed from prior guidance of "additional marketing investments" and staying within "10% to 12% of revenue" (CFO Taleghani, prior transcript) to now expecting marketing at a lower percentage of revenue and the "lower end" of 10% to 11% (CEO Plank; CFO Taleghani).
  • Current Q&A centered on a more promotional environment and traffic softness starting "mid- to late May" (CEO Plank); prior quarter Q&A leaned more toward defining “stabilization,” gross margin drivers, and e-commerce reset plans.

Risks and Concerns

  • "Traffic softened" and the marketplace became "increasingly promotional" in North America and Asia Pacific. (CEO Plank)
  • China challenges included "stock-outs" and "demand cannibalization from certain licensees that discounted aggressively"; management said it is being addressed through "better inventory availability and closer alignment with licensing partners." (CFO Taleghani)
  • Supply chain risk was flagged as "pressure related to the Middle East conflict" and tariff uncertainty, with management reiterating a "10% tariff assumption" through fiscal year-end. (CFO Taleghani)

Final Takeaway

Management said it is resetting Under Armour toward fewer, higher-impact products and more disciplined marketplace execution, cutting the full-year revenue outlook to a mid-single-digit decline while holding adjusted operating income guidance at $140 million to $160 million. Executives emphasized full-price demand creation (highlighting the $65 Bouncy Tee), targeted additional SKU reductions over the next 18 months, tighter SG&A control, and a shift to more efficient marketing spend, while citing softer traffic trends since late May and heightened promotional pressure—especially in North America, parts of Asia Pacific, and the U.K./Europe.

data.title: Ready Capital outlines $1.5B SBA 7(a) origination target as it reaches 81% of liquidity objective
data.description:
Earnings Call Insights: Ready Capital Corporation (RC) Q2 2026

Management View

  • "The second quarter of 2026 demonstrates meaningful progress in our balance sheet repositioning strategy" (Chairman, CEO & Chief Investment Officer Thomas Capasse), adding, "we do not anticipate further large portfolio sales" and "we have been organizing our work this year around 4 priorities" including "strengthening liquidity," "resolving non and subperforming CRE assets," "transitioning to a lower-cost business model," and "focusing on growth in our small business SBA 7(a) lending."
  • "Since our first quarter earnings" the company completed actions including "the sale of our $167 million construction portfolio," "the securitization of $158 million of unguaranteed SBA 7(a) loans at a 92% advance priced at SOFR plus 240 basis points," "the disposition of $445 million of CRE assets," and "the successful refinance of the Portland Ritz asset into a CPACE loan" (Chairman, CEO & Chief Investment Officer Capasse). He said these actions "have generated approximately $1.9 billion of cash" and "we now have achieved approximately 81% of our target liquidity objective."
  • "The current earnings drag across our non and subperforming and REO was $0.29 per share in the quarter" (Chairman, CEO & Chief Investment Officer Capasse). On SBA 7(a), he said Q2 originations were constrained, but "we expect steady growth towards our annual target of $1.5 billion of originations" and "we intend to accelerate our capital levels through more frequent SBA 7(a) ABS offerings."
  • "For the quarter, we reported a GAAP loss from continuing operations of $0.63 per common share" (CFO & Secretary Andrew Ahlborn). He added, "distributable earnings were a loss of $0.47 per common share" and "book value per share was $6.83 versus $7.43 at March 31."

Outlook

  • Management did not provide explicit EPS or revenue guidance in the prepared remarks or Q&A.
  • "We are no longer budgeting loan sales at this stage" (Chairman, CEO & Chief Investment Officer Capasse), framing remaining liquidity drivers as "the optimization of financing on $950 million of performing and nonperforming loans and runoff on $900 million, and a potential sale or financing on a $118 million joint venture position," which he said "will generate liquidity in excess of the 2026 remaining maturities."
  • "Those 3 things will result in a targeted 25% to 35% reduction in OpEx" (Chairman, CEO & Chief Investment Officer Capasse), tied to "divestiture of ancillary businesses" and "integration with the external manager's CRE lending businesses to source investments."

Financial Results

  • "Recurring revenue was $15.3 million compared to $16.2 million in the prior quarter" (CFO & Secretary Ahlborn). He attributed the shift to "an $8.7 million improvement in the net interest loss" offset by "a $2 million reduction in gain on sale revenue" and "a $7.5 million reduction in other recurring revenue."
  • "Operating expenses improved to $48.7 million from $67.7 million" (CFO & Secretary Ahlborn), primarily from "normalization of servicing expenses to $3.4 million from $15.4 million" after Q1 items related to "nonrecurring servicer advance reimbursements tied to the first quarter CLO collapses."
  • "We ended the quarter with $124.1 million of unrestricted cash" (CFO & Secretary Ahlborn). He also said "total assets declined to $6.26 billion" and "total leverage was 3x, trending towards our 2.5x target," with "$690 million of unencumbered assets."

Q&A

  • Crispin Love, Piper Sandler & Co.: "on meeting the fourth quarter debt maturities, can you share just what else needs to be done" and "what are you targeting for the remainder of 2026 as it relates for CRE and ... dispositions and runoff?" Chairman, CEO & Chief Investment Officer Capasse replied, "we're in the ... eighth inning" and said the plan centers on "optimization" of financing on "$950 million" of loans, "runoff on $900 million," and action on the "$118 million joint venture position," with loan sales only "opportunistically."
  • Crispin Love, Piper Sandler & Co.: asked about "potential monetization" of the Portland mixed-use property; Chairman, CEO & Chief Investment Officer Capasse said "that will lead to a decision to monetize it at some point in the next ... coming quarters," describing "linear improvement" at the hotel and progress on condo sell-through.
  • Jade Rahmani, KBW: asked, "Can you say more about the $118 million joint venture investment?" Chairman, CEO & Chief Investment Officer Capasse said it is "essentially an LP interest in a Waterfall-managed CRE fund" and later added it is "a straight-up LP interest in a fund that's in its harvest period" and that the company is evaluating "fund financing on LP interest as well as a secondary market for sale."
  • Jade Rahmani, KBW: questioned leverage on the CRE book and the feasibility of avoiding asset sales; CFO & Secretary Ahlborn said asset-level "average advance rates ... are in the low 60s" and described corporate secured debt as "equity pledges of entities throughout the structure." Chairman, CEO & Chief Investment Officer Capasse responded, "we constantly evaluate ... the discount for sale in the secondary market versus on-balance sheet strategies" and said there is "a lot of liquidity available for these assets."
  • Jade Rahmani, KBW: asked whether the company can return to profitability; Chairman, CEO & Chief Investment Officer Capasse answered, "Yes," outlining "the runoff of the legacy book," ramping SBA (which he called "highly profitable"), and the targeted OpEx reduction.

Sentiment Analysis

  • Analysts: slightly negative to skeptical, highlighted by Jade Rahmani’s comment, "it seems challenging to raise $450 million of equity capital" and surprise at reduced emphasis on loan sales.
  • Management: slightly positive in prepared remarks and steady in Q&A, using confidence language such as "we're confident" and "we're highly confident" (Chairman, CEO & Chief Investment Officer Capasse), while CFO Ahlborn emphasized "a deceleration in the pressures" on results.
  • Versus last quarter, management messaging shifted from execution of large loan sales to stressing fewer sales and more financing/runoff, while analyst questioning remained focused on liquidity, leverage, and asset quality.

Quarter-over-Quarter Comparison

  • Q1 emphasized liquidity from loan sales: "we made the decision to delever the balance sheet with aggressive asset management focused primarily on loan sales" (Chairman, CEO & Chief Investment Officer Capasse, Q1). In Q2, management pivoted: "we do not anticipate further large portfolio sales" and "we are no longer budgeting loan sales" (Chairman, CEO & Chief Investment Officer Capasse, Q2).
  • The Ritz/Portland asset narrative evolved from progress metrics to monetization timing: Q2 added, "determine the optimal path forward ... whether that's continued stabilization or monetization" (Chairman, CEO & Chief Investment Officer Capasse).
  • SBA 7(a) shifted from pending capacity (Q1: "pending launch") to completed financing and a production target (Q2: "we expect steady growth towards our annual target of $1.5 billion of originations").

Risks and Concerns

  • "37% or roughly $1 billion of the loan book comprises sub and nonperforming assets" (Chairman, CEO & Chief Investment Officer Capasse), and he said the Ritz REO represents "approximately 22% of quarter end stockholders' equity."
  • Liquidity execution risk remains tied to specific actions: "optimizing the financing of approximately $950 million of CRE loans" and action on the "$118 million joint venture position" (Chairman, CEO & Chief Investment Officer Capasse).
  • Management’s mitigation centered on asset-level financing and operating cost reductions: "We are executing a targeted cost optimization program" (Chairman, CEO & Chief Investment Officer Capasse) and "we expect net interest income to continue improving as nonaccrual loans and REO are resolved" (CFO & Secretary Ahlborn).

Final Takeaway

Management characterized Q2 as progress in repositioning, stating it does not expect further large portfolio sales and instead plans to finish 2026 maturities through financing optimization, portfolio runoff, and potential monetization/financing of a joint venture LP interest. Leadership also tied a return to profitability to resolving legacy CRE/REO earnings drag, ramping SBA 7(a) toward a $1.5 billion annual origination target supported by ABS capacity, and implementing a targeted 25% to 35% operating expense reduction.

data.title: Geospace targets $10.8M U.S. Navy system completion by December 2027 amid PRM timing shift
data.description:
Earnings Call Insights: Geospace Technologies (GEOS) Q3 fiscal 2026

Management view

  • "For the 3 months ended June 30, 2026, we reported revenue of $15.8 million with a net loss of $9.7 million," said (President, CEO & Director Richard Kelley), adding that "challenging market conditions across our business segments continue to impact our short-term financial performance" and that margins were pressured by "product mix, inflation, raw material costs and component availability."

  • "Our Smart Water segment continued its dip in revenue, which is driven in large part by reduced orders of the Hydroconn connector," said (President, CEO & Director Kelley), and added, "In June, we announced the release of the Series V connector" and "we offer the most universally compatible portfolio of Smart Water meter connectors and adapters available domestically."

  • "At the end of the third quarter, our subsidiary, Quantum Technology Sciences, received a $10.8 million contract from the U.S. Navy to deliver the seismic acoustic detection and ranging system," said (President, CEO & Director Kelley), and noted, "This contract is expected to be completed by December 2027."

  • "Third quarter revenue contribution from the PRM contract or permanent reservoir monitoring contract was lower than was expected due to customer requested changes to the project scope," said (President, CEO & Director Kelley), while emphasizing, "Importantly, our customer agreed to extend the PRM contract period of performance to account for these modifications" and "We have now successfully entered full production of the goods contract."

  • "We will not provide any specific revenue or earnings guidance during our call this morning," said (Executive VP, CFO & Secretary Robert Curda), and added, "we reported revenue of $15.8 million compared to last year's revenue of $24.8 million" and "The net loss for the quarter was $9.7 million or $0.75 per diluted share compared to last year's net income of $800,000 or $0.06 per diluted share."

Outlook

  • "We will not provide any specific revenue or earnings guidance during our call this morning," said (Executive VP, CFO & Secretary Curda).

  • On PRM timing, "there's no financial impact to the contract. The total value remains the same," said (President, CEO & Director Kelley), and characterized the change as "just an extension on the period of performance" and "simply 1 quarter delay, everything else is the same."

  • On the next PRM opportunities, "they have not put forward when they anticipate releasing the next proposed PRM system," said (President, CEO & Director Kelley), adding, "as it stands right now, there is nothing firm on the calendar."

  • On the Navy program’s path beyond this award, "the Navy will use that to determine how they want to move forward in a larger scale," said (President, CEO & Director Kelley).

Financial results

  • "For the 9 months ending June 30, 2026, we reported revenue of $61.1 million compared to revenue of $80.1 million last year," said (Executive VP, CFO & Secretary Curda), adding, "Our net loss for the 9-month period was $30.5 million or $2.37 per diluted share compared to last year's net loss of $700,000 or $0.05 per diluted share."

  • Segment results were framed around demand softness: "The decline in revenue for the 3-month and 9-month period is due to lower demand for our Hydroconn connector product line," said (Executive VP, CFO & Secretary Curda); "The decrease in revenue for the 9-month period is attributed to lower demand for our ocean bottom nodal products," and the Intelligent Industrial decline was "driven by lower demand for our industrial sensors" and "decreased demand for our company's contract manufacturing services."

  • Cost and liquidity commentary focused on expense reductions and funding capacity: "Our operating expenses decreased by $1.2 million for the third quarter of 2026," said (Executive VP, CFO & Secretary Curda), and added, "we maintained available borrowings of $25 million" and "our working capital is $41 million, which includes $17 million of trade accounts and financing receivables."

Q&A

  • William Dezellem, Tieton Capital Management, LLC: "provide a lot more detail around those scope changes" on PRM; (President, CEO & Director Kelley): "there's no financial impact to the contract. The total value remains the same" and "it's just an extension on the period of performance."

  • William Dezellem, Tieton Capital Management, LLC: implications for competitiveness; (President, CEO & Director Kelley): "Quite honestly, Bill, no" and "there was no technical change to the equipment that we're providing."

  • William Dezellem, Tieton Capital Management, LLC: next PRM contract visibility; (President, CEO & Director Kelley): "there is nothing firm on the calendar" and "we do anticipate participating in any proposal they put out."

  • William Dezellem, Tieton Capital Management, LLC: Navy contract and follow-ons; (President, CEO & Director Kelley): "there's only so much we can share" and "the Navy will use that to determine how they want to move forward in a larger scale."

  • William Dezellem, Tieton Capital Management, LLC: revenue recognition mechanics (Navy/PRM); (President, CEO & Director Kelley): "It's a progress payment type structure" and "it will bridge a couple of fiscal years"; (Executive VP, CFO & Secretary Curda): "We will recognize revenue independent of the milestones we're paid, and we'll recognize revenue over time that's similar to percentage completion."

  • William Dezellem, Tieton Capital Management, LLC: PRM completion window after the scope change; (President, CEO & Director Kelley): "we're anticipating somewhere between our fiscal Q3 and fiscal Q4 of next year" and clarified "Fiscal '27."

  • William Dezellem, Tieton Capital Management, LLC: heartbeat detector update; (President, CEO & Director Kelley): "We've done several pilots" and "I think we're actually a little bit ahead of our plan" while noting sales "does take some time" given "government agencies."

  • William Dezellem, Tieton Capital Management, LLC: cash burn concerns; (Executive VP, CFO & Secretary Curda): "We're managing cash very closely" and "we're getting a group together to analyze expenses" and "I think we're going to be in a good shape with the help of our bank -- our credit facility."

Sentiment analysis

  • Analysts were pointed and risk-focused, including timing/visibility and liquidity, with the question, "there is some concern about the cash burn rate," from William Dezellem, Tieton Capital Management, LLC.

  • Management’s tone in prepared remarks was cautious on near-term conditions ("challenging market conditions"), while responses in Q&A emphasized certainty where possible ("no financial impact," "total value remains the same") and limited disclosure on defense work ("there's only so much we can share").

  • Versus the prior quarter, the Q3 discussion shifted from restructuring and early PRM execution milestones to explaining a PRM schedule adjustment and addressing cash management more directly.

Quarter-over-quarter comparison

  • Q3 results included "revenue of $15.8 million" and "a net loss of $9.7 million" (President, CEO & Director Kelley) versus Q2’s "revenue of $19.7 million with a net loss of $11.1 million" (President, CEO & Director Kelley).

  • Smart Water commentary evolved from Q2’s "customers work through excess inventory" (Executive VP, CFO & Secretary Curda) to Q3’s "reduced orders of the Hydroconn connector" and a product response with "the release of the Series V connector" (President, CEO & Director Kelley).

  • PRM messaging shifted from Q2’s "recognized our first revenue" and a longer-duration view ("late in 2027 or early of 2028," said (Executive VP, CFO & Secretary Curda) in Q2) to Q3’s emphasis on a scope-driven delay but "no financial impact" and an expected wrap of revenue recognition "between our fiscal Q3 and fiscal Q4 of next year" (President, CEO & Director Kelley).

Risks and concerns

  • "Revenue was impacted by geopolitical uncertainty, project timing, sales volumes and customer access to capital," said (President, CEO & Director Kelley), and added that margins were pressured by "inflation" and "component availability," with mitigation including "cost reduction efforts and improvements in manufacturing productivity."

  • Contract timing and customer-driven changes remained a key execution risk: "customer requested changes to the project scope" reduced expected PRM revenue contribution in the quarter (President, CEO & Director Kelley), though management said the customer "agreed to extend" the period of performance.

  • Liquidity and burn-rate attention surfaced in Q&A, with (Executive VP, CFO & Secretary Curda) stating, "We're managing cash very closely" and pointing to "our credit facility" as support.

Final takeaway

Management described a quarter pressured by lower Hydroconn demand, softer seismic acquisition equipment demand, and PRM timing changes, while pointing to two major forward-looking items: a $10.8 million U.S. Navy award expected to complete by December 2027 and continued PRM execution with "no financial impact" but a schedule extension. In Q&A, discussion centered on PRM timing and visibility, defense contract scope, and cash management actions, with the CFO emphasizing close cash control and reliance on the credit facility as the company works toward future milestone-driven cash inflows.

data.title: Fed's hawkish stance likely intact despite soft jobs data - strategist
data.description:
In a sharp departure from consensus market views, Skanda Amarnath, executive director at Employ America, argued Friday that the July jobs report carries distinctly "hawkish implications" for the Federal Reserve.

While many investors viewed recent weaker payroll numbers as a sign of economic cooling, Amarnath is contending that the underlying data suggests the labor market remains balanced, offering central bank officials little reason to adopt a dovish stance.

Nonfarm payrolls dropped by 23K jobs in July, an unexpectedly weak print that was compounded by a severe 103K downward revision for May and June combined, sparking investor optimism that the Federal Reserve will hold off on imminent interest rate hikes.

Amarnath highlighted several critical factors driving his outlook, starting with a 4.1% unemployment rate that represents a clear downward inflection year-to-date. He attributed the recent softness in payrolls largely to temporary seasonal adjustment quirks—particularly within local government education, which alone shaved off roughly 50K jobs.

Furthermore, because the Fed maintains a low breakeven threshold for payroll growth, Amarnath stressed that the recent revisions are simply not soft enough to prompt a shift toward rate cuts.

With Fed officials already lowering their threshold for policy tightening after underreacting to prior inflation spikes, Amarnath warned that markets expecting an imminent pivot may be misinterpreting the central bank's reaction function.

data.title: Instacart's AI assistant: If they build it, bigger baskets will come
data.description:
Driven by advertising gains and higher order values, Instacart (CART) beat Wall Street’s expectations for the second quarter and set its third quarter guidance to reflect the gains in the business during the first half of the year.

The next phase of growth for the grocery delivery business now shifts to its investment in artificial intelligence and its potential to lure in new cohorts and create larger basket sizes.

“In our view, the grocery category is well suited for AI innovation given inventory and shopping complexities,” notes BofA Securities analyst Justin Post.

“Orders placed with the assistance have larger than average [average order values], and a broader rollout could be a catalyst for the stock,” Post added.

According to Post, the fact that Instacart (CART) has delivered double-digit growth for five straight quarters speaks to the “stickiness” of large baskets, a phenomenon that will be amplified by AI. “Tell AI what you want to cook, and it can build the list and order ingredients,” Post notes.

Oppenheimer analyst Jason Helfstein agrees, noting that AI assistant orders are driving larger basket sizes than the corporate average.

Moreover, accelerating gross transaction value ((GTV)) and AOVs will help Instacart (CART) maintain its healthy margins and remain competitive in the online grocery delivery business.

Instacart CEO Chris Rogers also noted the larger basket size generated by the AI assistant and its potential going forward. 

“We believe that AI is going to be a meaningful growth driver for us and for the category. Our AI assistant delivers an agentic experience that’s intended to remove the friction [of time constraints, dietary restrictions, and personal tastes], and it’s making shopping more personalized and intuitive,” Rogers said on the company's earnings call.

The company plans to launch its AI assistant across the Instacart marketplace in North America over the next several weeks.

data.title: Midday Need to Know: Payrolls fall, Lilly and Novo win antitrust battle & more
data.description:
Wall Street’s major market averages traded towards the topside on Friday after July's nonfarm payrolls surprised to the downside, showing an unexpected contraction in employment.

The blue-chip Dow (DJI) was last +0.1%, the benchmark S&P 500 (SP500) was last +0.3%, and the tech-focused Nasdaq Composite (COMP:IND) was last +0.7%.

Now, here are four news stories that broke in the morning to watch out for:

Payrolls trigger rate pause: U.S. nonfarm payrolls fell by 23,000 in July, missing the +88,000 consensus and marking the first decline since June's revised gain of just 20,000. Revisions to the prior two months stripped another 103,000 jobs combined, with May slashed to +63,000 from +129,000. The unemployment rate dipped to 4.1% from 4.2%, though labor force participation fell to 61.4%, the lowest since February 2021. Average hourly earnings rose just 0.1% month-over-month, bringing the year-over-year gain to 3.2%, the weakest in five years. Markets responded by lifting the probability of a Fed rate hold at 3.50%-3.75% to 55.9% from 45.0% the prior day, according to the CME FedWatch tool.

Take-Two schedules GTA 6: Take-Two Interactive Software  (TTWO)  confirmed Grand Theft Auto 6 will launch on November 19 for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S, reiterating full-year FY27 net bookings guidance of $8.0 billion to $8.2 billion. Q1 net bookings of $1.39 billion topped the $1.37 billion consensus, while GAAP EPS of -$0.18 beat the -$0.21 estimate. Freedom Capital Markets forecasts 30 million units in the launch quarter, noting the franchise has grown substantially since GTA V sold nearly 29 million copies in about six weeks following its 2013 release. Shares fell 1.4% in premarket trading and are down more than 9% year-to-date.

Lilly and Novo win antitrust battle: A federal judge in Texas  dismissed an antitrust lawsuit brought by compounding pharmacy Strive Specialties against Eli Lilly  (LLY) and Novo Nordisk (NVO) over their GLP-1 drugs. Judge Micaela Alvarez ruled Strive failed to prove antitrust injuries because its compounded versions do not operate in the same market as Lilly's Zepbound and Novo's Wegovy. Strive had alleged the drugmakers blocked access to customized versions through exclusive telehealth partnerships. Lilly called the claim "meritless," while Strive said it was weighing an appeal.

FAA orders Boeing inspections: The Federal Aviation Administration  ordered safety inspections of 471 Boeing 737 MAX jets in the U.S. after cracks were discovered in structural reinforcement around service doors on older plane models. The directive covers 737-8, 737-9, and 737-8200 variants. Boeing said the issue has not been observed on the MAX fleet but extended inspections because the model shares a similar design and build process with older jets. The directive comes less than a month after the FAA restored Boeing's authority to conduct final safety signoffs on newly produced 737s.

data.title: Tandem forecasts $265M Q3 sales while advancing Mobi tubeless scaled launch in H2 2026
data.description:
Earnings Call Insights: Tandem Diabetes Care (TNDM) Q2 2026

Management View

  • “The second quarter marked an important step forward for Tandem. We are executing against our strategic priorities while demonstrating operational momentum, improving our financial performance, and providing broader access to our technology.” (President, CEO & Director John Sheridan)
  • “We now have approximately 45% formulary coverage, which is already approaching the high end of our range for the goals this year.” (President Sheridan)
  • “In our first full quarter offering PAYGO, U.S. sales through the pharmacy channel increased to 10%.” (President Sheridan)
  • “We reached an important R&D milestone in Q2 with a 510(k) submission for Mobi tubeless.” (President Sheridan)
  • “To support this, we are launching AutoSoft Plus… and plan to expand to additional geographies, including the U.S. later this year.” (President Sheridan)
  • “Over the past 2 years… culminating in FDA approval of an IDE in Q2 and positioning us to begin a pivotal study later this year.” (President Sheridan)
  • “Worldwide sales totaled $255 million, increasing 6% year-over-year or 5% in constant currency.” (Executive VP, CFO & Treasurer Leigh Vosseller)
  • “Gross margin was 57%, improving 5 percentage points year-over-year and 2 points sequentially.” (Executive VP Vosseller)

Outlook

  • “For the third quarter, worldwide sales are expected to be approximately $265 million.” (Executive VP Vosseller)
  • “Worldwide sales are expected to be in the range of $1.065 billion to $1.085 billion.” (Executive VP Vosseller)
  • “We expect gross margins in the range of 56% to 57% and adjusted EBITDA margin of 5% to 6% of annual sales.” (Executive VP Vosseller)
  • “Gross margin is expected to be approximately 56% and adjusted EBITDA margin approximately 2% of sales.” (Executive VP Vosseller)
  • Compared with Q1, management again “reaffirm[ed]” full-year sales and margin guidance, while Q2 commentary emphasized that PAYGO is in its “first full quarter” with “sales through the pharmacy… 10%,” versus Q1’s description of early weeks where “Fewer than 5% of customers ordered a pump through their pharmacy benefit.” (Executive VP Vosseller)

Financial Results

  • “We shipped approximately 33,000 pumps worldwide.” (Executive VP Vosseller)
  • “In the U.S., we shipped a Q2 record of 22,000 pumps, growing 7% year-over-year.” (Executive VP Vosseller)
  • “In the second quarter, the initial headwind from pharmacy pumps was approximately $8 million.” (Executive VP Vosseller)
  • “International sales totaled $75 million, increasing 7% year-over-year or 6% in constant currency.” (Executive VP Vosseller)
  • “Operating expenses were $159 million, remaining relatively flat year-over-year.” (Executive VP Vosseller)
  • “We ended the quarter with a healthy balance sheet including $456 million in cash and investments compared to $570 million at the end of Q1.” (Executive VP Vosseller)

Q&A

  • Mathew Blackman, TD Cowen: asked about “areas… of friction in the pharmacy transition” and confidence in targets for “20% of pump shipments through the pharmacy.” President Sheridan: “there was nothing that was surprising. We feel like we're on track.”
  • Felipe Lamar, Truist: asked about “retention issues in the Type 2 community.” President Sheridan: “our Type 2 attrition, it's really modestly higher than our Type 1 rate, and it's been stable over the past 5 years.”
  • Larry Biegelsen, Wells Fargo: pressed on second-half drivers to hit U.S. pump guidance. Executive VP Vosseller: “we have a number of new products under launch right now… FreeStyle Libre 3… Mobi Android… pharmacy.”
  • Matthew O’Brien, Piper Sandler: asked why gross margin guide was reiterated and why Q3 steps down. Executive VP Vosseller: “we guided to a point step down in Q3, but still achieving that 60% gross margin in the fourth quarter.”
  • Joanne Wuensch, Citi: asked whether tubeless Mobi was filed and timing. President Sheridan: “we have filed it… we are planning on having clearance and actually beginning the scaling launch in the second half of this year.”
  • Jonathan Block, Stifel: asked whether higher pharmacy pricing implied supply conversions lagging. Executive VP Vosseller: “the pump adoption slightly outpaced… the supply side… that may continue into the third quarter.”

Sentiment Analysis

  • Analysts’ tone was slightly negative to pressing around execution risk and pacing, including “friction in the pharmacy transition,” implied shipment softness, and whether pharmacy conversion cadence is realistic.
  • Management’s tone was slightly positive and confident, repeatedly using conviction language such as “we feel like we're on track” and “we remain confident,” while acknowledging operational pacing effects like “pump adoption… outpaced… the supply side.”
  • Versus Q1’s early-stage framing (“still early in the process”), Q2 kept a similar confidence level but leaned more on tangible traction (“sales through the pharmacy… 10%”) and reiterated margin pathway (“still achieving that 60% gross margin in the fourth quarter”).

Quarter-over-Quarter Comparison

  • PAYGO progressed from Q1’s “Fewer than 5%” pharmacy pump and supply adoption to Q2’s “sales through the pharmacy increased to 10%,” alongside formulary coverage moving from “approximately 40%” to “approximately 45%.” (Executive VP Vosseller; Executive VP Vosseller; President Sheridan)
  • Tubeless Mobi moved from Q1 planning (“We plan to file our 510(k) submission… in the second quarter”) to Q2 completion (“a 510(k) submission for Mobi tubeless”). (President Sheridan)
  • International go-direct messaging stayed consistent, but Q2 highlighted incremental timing headwinds (“$3 million… distributor inventory buybacks”) versus Q1 discussing timing of go-direct headwinds shifting into Q2. (Executive VP Vosseller)

Risks and Concerns

  • “We continue to manage shortages from our key infusion set supplier. We believe Q2 was the period of greatest impact, and our supplier expects availability to improve through the second half of the year.” (President Sheridan)
  • “Pump shipments through the pharmacy channels do not include upfront reimbursement, which creates a near-term headwind to revenue.” (Executive VP Vosseller)
  • “There’s still uncertainty from the FDA” on tubeless Mobi timing, with launch described as a “scaled launch” in the second half. (President Sheridan)

Final Takeaway

Management characterized Q2 as a step-up in execution, highlighting PAYGO traction (10% pharmacy mix and 45% formulary coverage), gross margin expansion to 57%, and a filed 510(k) for Mobi tubeless ahead of a planned scaled launch in the second half of 2026. Leadership also reaffirmed full-year sales and margin ranges while flagging near-term headwinds from pharmacy accounting dynamics and infusion-set supply constraints that they expect to ease through the second half.

data.title: Weak jobs report backs Fed pause as inflation takes center stage, Kelly and Hatzius - CNBC
data.description:
July's weak jobs report supported a Fed pause, while inflation remained the key policy driver, David Kelly and Jan Hatzius said in separate CNBC interviews.

Hatzius called the payrolls report “weaker” overall, saying Goldman Sachs' composite measure of underlying job growth had slowed to about 5K from just over 70K before the report after incorporating the latest data and revisions.

"The biggest takeaway" was the sharp slowdown in underlying job growth, Hatzius said. While the household survey was more mixed, he said recent declines in labor force participation suggested some labor market weakness, even though demographic changes and updated Census estimates had also affected the data.

Kelly described the labor market as “not strong” but "tight," arguing that businesses continued to struggle to find workers while employees lacked the bargaining power to demand significantly higher wages.

"That's why we've got Teflon inflation here," Kelly said. "In order to get a wage-price spiral, you've got to get the wages to go up, and that's not happening."

Both economists said inflation would be the bigger driver of the Fed's next decision. Hatzius said next week's inflation report would show whether June's benign reading had been "a one-off or maybe the start of a softer trend," adding that one month of data was insufficient to draw firm conclusions.

Looking ahead, Kelly said Fed Chair Kevin Warsh would likely have to offer clearer guidance at the Jackson Hole symposium.

"You really need to communicate," Kelly said. "Uncertainty is sand in the gears of the economy."

Hatzius said policymakers were likely to continue expressing differing views ahead of the September meeting, but he expected inflation data to remain benign enough for the Fed to leave rates unchanged.

U.S. nonfarm payrolls declined by 23K in July, missing the +88K consensus and erasing the 20K increase in June, according to data released by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics on Friday. What's more, June's growth was scaled back by more than half from the initial print of 57K. Unemployment slipped to 4.1% from 4.2% in June, lower than the 4.2% consensus.
